wiki-iran.standing: A daily count of how many people open the Wikipedia article on Iran — a rough gauge of how much of the world is trying to understand the country at once. It rises with wars, strikes and negotiations, and falls back within days.
wiki-iran.recent: The peak passed as the confrontation moved to the table: Trump halted the attack on Iran's infrastructure on 2 August, and Oman, not Washington, is now brokering the strait's reopening. The pressure has not lifted — Hormuz transits fell by a third this week, and Treasury sanctioned a dollar-token exchange serving Iran.

brent.standing: The price of a barrel of North Sea crude, and the benchmark most of the world's oil is sold against. It moves on supply — a strike, a sanction, a strait — and fuel, freight and fertiliser move after it.
brent.recent: Crude has come off its highs as the Strait of Hormuz edges toward reopening: Oman is brokering talks, and Trump halted planned attacks on Iran's infrastructure. Supply risk persists — Houthi missiles hit Marib, Ukraine struck the Yaroslavl refinery, and a Senate bill would tax buyers of Russian oil.

wti.standing: The price of a barrel of West Texas Intermediate, the light sweet crude that sets the US benchmark and prices most North American oil. It moves on supply and policy, and fuel, freight and plastics move after it.
wti.recent: Crude fell 4.5% after a remark on Iran drained the war premium, and a treasury secretary's Hormuz deal claim reversed the gains that followed. OPEC+ then hiked output by 188,000 barrels daily, leaving the price near $82 despite Ukrainian strikes on two Russian refineries.

natgas-hh.standing: The US benchmark price for natural gas, set at a Louisiana pipeline junction and used to price most American gas contracts. It sets what US power plants, fertiliser makers and heating bills pay, and anchors the export price of American LNG.
natgas-hh.recent: Henry Hub has drifted down through the summer to a low on Jul 29, and the war-risk events in the gas trade sat outside the US market: a drone strike set fire to tankers at Egypt's Damietta LNG port on the same day, and vessels there were hit again days later. Domestic demand news ran the other way, with SpaceX building its own gas plants for a Texas chip factory.

wheat.standing: The export price of a tonne of milling wheat, the world's most traded food grain. It sets the cost of bread in countries that import it in dollars and sell it subsidised at home, so a move here reaches the poorest tables first.
wheat.recent: European and Black Sea heatwaves cut yields while war-driven freight and insurance costs rose on every tonne shipped, stacking a delivery shock on a supply shock. The FAO's food price index hit 131.1 on 7 August, a three-and-a-half-year high led by cereals — the line that dominates the import bill in Egypt, Pakistan, Nigeria and Bangladesh.

rice.standing: The export price of milled rice, the staple calorie for more than half the world. It trades thinly, so one exporter's ban or a monsoon that arrives wrong moves it fast — and it passes straight into the food-import bills of Asia and West Africa.
rice.recent: Rice has diverged from the rest of the basket. It sits near 400, well below its 2024 peak of 563.8, even as the Food and Agriculture Organization's price index reached 131.1 — a rise driven by cereals and vegetable oils rather than by the grain most of Asia eats.

copper.standing: The price of a tonne of refined copper, the metal that carries current in every grid, motor and building. Demand for it tracks electrification and construction, and supply sits with a handful of mines, which is why it is read as a gauge of industrial growth.
copper.recent: The rise runs alongside a surge in electrical demand the grids cannot meet: ERCOT froze new data-centre connections with 474 gigawatts of requests queued, five times peak demand, and one US outage cut power to 67 million customers. Vehicle electrification is compounding it — Tata's EV sales doubled in July.

us-10y.standing: The yield on ten-year US government debt — the price at which the world's largest borrower funds itself, and the benchmark against which mortgages, corporate bonds and sovereign debt everywhere are priced. It rises when investors demand more to hold duration.
us-10y.recent: The yield climbed toward its 31 July high while the Fed held rates at 350-375 basis points, citing elevated inflation — a supply-shock regime in which war-driven energy and freight costs push prices up as demand softens. Traders had been pricing a hike; by 7 August the dollar fell to its weakest since May as that hike came into doubt.

sp500.standing: A capitalisation-weighted index of 500 large US companies, and the default measure of American equity performance. Because pensions and index funds worldwide track it, its level sets the value of retirement savings far beyond the United States.
sp500.recent: The index sits at a high after a run in which the market's AI trade was repeatedly questioned rather than abandoned: Alphabet's stock fell 7% on the same capex it used to cheer, a fund built on AI conviction sold AI, and Microsoft then topped quarterly cloud growth estimates, easing spending concerns. The Fed held interest rates steady citing 'elevated' inflation.

nasdaq100.standing: A stock index tracking the 100 largest non-financial companies on the Nasdaq exchange, weighted by market value. It is dominated by a handful of US technology firms, so it moves less on the American economy than on what happens to them.
nasdaq100.recent: The index sits near the top of its 62-day range after a late-July trough, with the largest constituents absorbing a run of legal and structural news: a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $567 million over product design in a child safety case, with $420 million ring-fenced for treatment, and Google set 4 September as the date Assistant is replaced by Gemini.

us-gas-retail.standing: The average pump price of a gallon of regular gasoline across the United States, surveyed weekly. It tracks crude oil with a lag, plus refining margins and state taxes, and it is the price most American households feel first when oil markets move.
us-gas-retail.recent: Prices have eased through the summer despite mounting damage to refining capacity: Ukrainian drones hit two Russian refineries on 6 August, a second strike at Yaroslavl since July, after an earlier attack at Ryazan, while Houthi strikes shut Aramco's 400,000-bpd Jazan refinery. The hits fall on refining, not crude supply.

natgas-ttf.standing: The price of gas delivered into northwest Europe's TTF hub, the continent's benchmark since it replaced Russian pipeline contracts as the reference for imported LNG. It sets what factories, power stations and households pay, and it moves on weather, storage and shipping.
natgas-ttf.recent: Gas has climbed roughly a quarter over the window, holding near the March 2026 high of $17.67 against a December low of $9.46. The drone strike on floating storage at Egypt's Damietta LNG terminal on 29 July, where fire spread from one tanker to a second, put Mediterranean cargoes and war-risk cover on the route in question.

vix.standing: A measure of how much movement traders are paying for in S&P 500 options over the coming month, derived from those option prices rather than from the index itself. It rises when investors bid up protection, which is why it is read as the market's price of fear.
vix.recent: Volatility has drained out of risk markets rather than spiked: spot bitcoin ETFs absorbed $754 million in the first week of August with no outflow days and the price barely moved, a market with depth but no direction. The same pattern of suppressed realised volatility alongside bid-up downside protection sits under the equity gauge.

fx-pkr.standing: The exchange rate between Pakistan's rupee and the US dollar, and the price at which the country buys its fuel, food and machinery. Pakistan imports far more than it exports, so the rate sets the cost of living and the weight of its dollar debt.
fx-pkr.recent: The rupee has been close to flat over the past month, easing from 279.2 on 14 July to 276.8. The State Bank held its policy rate at 11.5% on 27 July, with imported inflation and debt service the stated concerns, and the finance ministry has since put its inflation forecast at 9-10% on the back of a war shock.

fx-ngn.standing: Nigeria's currency, quoted as naira per US dollar, so a higher number means a weaker naira. Africa's largest economy imports most of its fuel and much of its food, so this rate sets domestic prices and the cost of servicing foreign debt.
fx-ngn.recent: The naira traded in a narrow band through the month, weakest at 1386 on Jul 14 and strongest at 1358 on Jul 31, finishing marginally firmer than it began. No policy decision or market event in the record accounts for the drift.

fx-egp.standing: Egypt's currency against the US dollar. A managed float that the central bank has devalued repeatedly to secure IMF money and clear import backlogs, it sets the price of the wheat, fuel and medicine Egypt buys abroad — and so the cost of living for a country that imports most of what it eats.
fx-egp.recent: The pound has firmed from 51.37 on 25 July to 49.56, roughly a tenth of its value recovered in two weeks. The move follows a run of strain rather than calm: a drone strike on energy vessels at Damietta days after Europe staked its gas supply on the port, and a 5.5-magnitude earthquake near Suez felt in Cairo. The domestic cost is visible at the pharmacy counter, where a pricing freeze has emptied shelves.

fx-try.standing: The Turkish lira against the US dollar. A managed float with persistent depreciation, it prices imported energy and food for 85 million people and is the channel through which Ankara's rate and reserve decisions reach household costs.
fx-try.recent: The lira slid to 47.7 per dollar on Aug 7 as Turkey pulled deeper into the Black Sea war's economic front: drones struck the Turkish-operated Nadezhda near Novorossiysk on Aug 4, and Turkey's coast guard began turning back some vessels bound for the port. The same day, Ankara signed a joint defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan in Mecca.

fx-bdt.standing: The exchange rate of Bangladesh's currency against the US dollar, quoted as taka per dollar, so a rising number means a weaker taka. It sets the cost of the fuel, food and industrial inputs a garment-exporting economy has to import.
fx-bdt.recent: The taka drifted about a quarter of a percent weaker over the month, from 122.7 on Jul 16 to a high of 124 on Aug 7, with no single event in the record behind the move. The window covered a diplomatic run between Dhaka and Delhi over Hasina's planned address and the unsigned Teesta water treaty, neither of which is a currency story.

fx-idr.standing: The exchange rate between Indonesia's rupiah and the US dollar, quoted as rupiah per dollar, so a rising number means a weaker rupiah. It is Southeast Asia's most commodity-exposed major currency and sets the local cost of imported fuel, food and dollar debt.
fx-idr.recent: The rupiah has recovered from its Jul 13 level of 18,140 to 17,800, its strongest in the month, despite the surprise mid-term resignation of Bank Indonesia governor Perry Warjiyo on Jul 27, which left the central bank without a named successor.

fx-lbp.standing: The Lebanese pound's exchange rate against the US dollar. The currency lost most of its value after Lebanon's 2019 banking collapse and now trades at a rate the central bank holds steady, so imported food, fuel and medicine are priced in dollars for a population paid in pounds.
fx-lbp.recent: The pound barely moved through a month in which the ceasefire in the south broke down repeatedly: Israeli strikes on a cemetery prayer area near Tibnin killed one, a bomb killed three, and demolitions in southern Lebanon registered magnitude 3.8. A seventh round of direct talks opened in Rome on Tuesday. The rate held near its 30-day range.

fx-cny.standing: China's currency against the US dollar, managed within a daily band the People's Bank of China sets rather than floated freely. It is the price at which the world's largest exporter of manufactured goods gets paid, so it prices everything from solar panels to shipping contracts.
fx-cny.recent: The yuan drifted to the strong end of its month, 6.747 on Aug 8 against a Jul 10 high of 6.784 — a move of roughly half a percent, which is quiet. Nothing in the month's China news explains it: Beijing sanctioned six US entities and tightened drone export controls, and Washington set a polysilicon price floor, but the currency barely registered either.

fx-inr.standing: The exchange rate between India's rupee and the US dollar, the price at which the world's most populous economy buys its oil, chips and machinery. A weaker rupee raises the cost of everything India imports, and the Reserve Bank of India spends reserves to slow the slide.
fx-inr.recent: The rupee has held in a narrow band, easing from 96.65 on 18 July to 95.05 on 5 August before settling at 95.14. The 4.5% fall in crude after a remark on Iran cut India's largest import bill, while a US Senate bill threatening 100% tariffs over purchases of Russian oil left the currency exposed to how New Delhi answers it.

fx-brl.standing: The exchange rate of Brazil's currency against the US dollar, quoted as reais per dollar, so a rising number means a weaker real. It prices the world's largest coffee, soy and iron-ore exporter, and moves on domestic politics as much as on commodity demand.
fx-brl.recent: The real held a narrow range through a deteriorating US-Brazil relationship: Brasília refused entry to two senior US diplomats on 25 July and filed for WTO consultations over US tariffs on 28 July, and Washington revoked the Brazilian ambassador's visa on 4 August. Lula was nominated for a fourth term on 2 August.

fx-mxn.standing: The Mexican peso against the US dollar, one of the most heavily traded emerging-market currencies and a round-the-clock proxy for sentiment on Mexico's economy and its relationship with Washington. Trade, remittances and manufacturing all price through it.
fx-mxn.recent: The peso firmed to 17.14 from a 17.54 peak on Jul 19, its strongest level in the window, through a month in which Mexico's news flow was security and public health rather than macro: the US posted a $25 million bounty on a CJNG leader, the Sinaloa Cartel split into warring factions, human screwworm cases passed 500, and Mexico and Peru restored diplomatic relations. None of that explains the move.

fx-eur.standing: The price of one euro in US dollars, the second most traded currency on earth and the exchange rate that sets the price of everything moving between the euro area and the dollar bloc. It moves on relative growth, rate expectations and political risk inside the union.
fx-eur.recent: The euro slipped to 0.8651 on Aug 8 from 0.8792 on Jul 26, a period in which Italy suspended Schengen and reimposed border checks against Spain, Spain answered with reciprocal controls, and two founding members of the free-movement area began policing each other's travellers over arrivals at Ceuta. Brussels has not acted.

fx-jpy.standing: The exchange rate between Japan's currency and the US dollar, quoted as yen per dollar, so a rising number means a weaker yen. It is the funding leg of the global carry trade and sets the translated earnings of Japan's exporters.
fx-jpy.recent: Tokyo sold dollars for yen hours before the Bank of Japan held rates at 1% on 31 July, taking the yen off its 163.9 low against the dollar. A joint US-Japan intervention on 3 August pushed the dollar to a one-month low, the first such confirmed move with Washington. Toyota's quarterly profit nearly doubled to $9.4 billion on the cheap yen.

fx-rub.standing: The exchange rate of Russia's currency against the dollar, and the clearest daily read on how sanctions, oil revenue and capital controls are landing on the Russian economy. It sets the price of imports for households and the value of every export receipt.
fx-rub.recent: The ruble weakened through early August as pressure converged on Russia's oil revenue. The Senate passed a bill taxing buyers of Russian oil, aimed at Moscow but landing on India, China and Turkey, and Ukraine struck two Russian refineries including Yaroslavl — the second such strike since July. It hit 83 on Aug 7, from 76 on Jul 10.

fx-zar.standing: The currency of South Africa, priced against the dollar. It is one of the most heavily traded emerging-market currencies and a standing proxy for global risk appetite, so it swings on commodity prices and offshore sentiment as much as on domestic policy.
fx-zar.recent: The rand firmed to 16.15 per dollar, its strongest of the past month, recovering from 16.83 on 25 July. Nothing in the domestic record explains the move: the period's news was procurement — a Prasa security-contract probe in Pretoria and eleven years of undelivered vet buses — alongside electricity bills rising up to 14% this month.

poly-fed-rate-hike-in-2026.standing: A Polymarket contract on whether the Federal Reserve raises its policy rate at any point in 2026. The price is what traders will pay for that outcome, so it reprices on inflation data, oil shocks and anything that changes who controls the Fed.
poly-fed-rate-hike-in-2026.recent: Odds peaked at 77 on Jul 28, the eve of a decision Citadel was betting would surprise markets with a hike, with investors pricing one in. The Fed instead held at 350-375 basis points, citing elevated inflation, and the bet has drained to 55 — though Trump's second move to fire Governor Lisa Cook reopened the independence fight.

poly-will-the-fed-increase-interest-rate.standing: A Polymarket contract on whether the US Federal Reserve raises its policy rate by 25 basis points at the meeting after September 2026. The price is what traders will pay for that outcome, so it moves as bets shift, not as forecasters revise.
poly-will-the-fed-increase-interest-rate.recent: The Fed held rates at 350-375 basis points on 29 July, citing elevated inflation, and the bets on a hike fell away from their 60 high on Aug 1. Citadel had bet the Fed would surprise markets with a hike; it did not. Trump's second move to fire Governor Lisa Cook on 7 August reopened the fight over Fed independence.

poly-iran-leadership-change-by-august-31.standing: A Polymarket contract on whether Iran's leadership changes by a set date. It prices political rupture in a country that sits on the Strait of Hormuz and supplies much of the world's oil transit risk, so it moves with war, negotiation and succession rumour alike.
poly-iran-leadership-change-by-august-31.recent: The bet has drained as the confrontation moved toward negotiation rather than collapse: Trump halted the planned attack on Iran's infrastructure, and Oman — not Washington — began brokering the strait's reopening, with officials describing progress on 4 August. Iran and Pakistan opened their border crossings around the clock. The contract has since fallen to 4%, its low of 2% falling on 3 August.

poly-will-mojtaba-khamenei-be-head-of-st.standing: A Polymarket contract on whether Mojtaba Khamenei, son of Iran's supreme leader, becomes the country's head of state by the end of 2026. It is a bet on succession at the top of a system where the leader is chosen by an appointed clerical body, not an election.
poly-will-mojtaba-khamenei-be-head-of-st.recent: The contract has drifted down over the month, hitting 85 on Aug 5 before falling back to 76 — a slide that tracks Iran's confrontation with Washington cooling rather than sharpening. Trump halted planned attacks on Iran's infrastructure on Aug 2, and by Aug 4 Oman was brokering talks on reopening the Strait of Hormuz that officials described as making progress.

poly-will-the-us-invade-iran-before-2027.standing: A Polymarket contract on whether the United States launches an invasion of Iran before 2027, priced as a percentage. It is what traders will pay for that outcome, so it moves with each escalation or de-escalation rather than with any official statement of intent.
poly-will-the-us-invade-iran-before-2027.recent: The odds fell from 32 on Jul 19 to 17 as talks brokered by Oman on reopening the Strait of Hormuz made progress and Trump halted attacks on Iran's infrastructure. Pressure has shifted to sanctions — Treasury designated Iran-linked crypto exchanges — though tanker crews reported explosions near Hormuz and transits fell by a third.

btc.standing: The price of one bitcoin, the oldest and largest cryptocurrency and the one every other digital asset is priced against. It is held as a savings instrument where banking is closed or currency is collapsing, and it trades all day, every day.
btc.recent: A run of security failures has dragged on the price rather than any macro shift: a Coldcard seed-entropy flaw swept 594 bitcoin from 500 unrelated wallets in 25 minutes, a further Coldcard hack drained $120 million, and a BTCPay Server flaw let attackers empty the Lightning nodes of Foundation and Citadel21. Bitcoin fell 4% against every other market signal and sits 49% below its record.

eth.standing: The second-largest cryptocurrency by value, and the settlement layer most dollar stablecoins and tokenised trading actually run on. Its price moves with speculative flows, but its throughput is a rough gauge of how much of that plumbing is in use.
eth.recent: Ether led the crypto market higher on 27 July, the day the series peaked at $1,952, with bitcoin trading around $65,500 as Hormuz hostilities paused and the Fed prepared a rate decision. The rise stalled after South Korea's worst market day in years and a stalled Clarity Act; the Senate has since taken only procedural votes on the bill, with stablecoin yield still unsettled.

paxg.standing: A tokenised claim on a fixed weight of gold, priced per troy ounce and redeemable for allocated bullion. It tracks the metal that investors buy when they doubt currencies, so it moves against the dollar and against confidence in sovereign debt.
paxg.recent: The bid has come from money leaving the dollar: US debt growth has pushed investors toward gold and bitcoin as a hedge against devaluation, and Binance opened gold and silver options after commodity futures drew billions in daily volume. Tether's excess reserves, part-backed by gold, halved to $4.11 billion from $8.23 billion.

xag.standing: A silver-backed token priced off the metal itself. Silver is both a monetary metal and an industrial input — solar cells, electrical contacts, brazing alloys — so its price answers to investors and to factories at the same time.
xag.recent: The window closes at $58.35, roughly half a percent above where it started, after a high of $60.05 on Jul 27. A single reading of $29.80 on Aug 6 sits far below every other point in the series. Nothing in the material at hand accounts for either move.

xmr.standing: A privacy-focused cryptocurrency that hides sender, receiver and amount by default, unlike Bitcoin's public ledger. That opacity makes it the settlement asset of choice for ransomware crews and darknet markets, and the reason exchanges in several jurisdictions have delisted it.
xmr.recent: The rise runs alongside a widening enforcement and threat picture around ransomware: a Ransom Cartel operator was sentenced in Washington on 6 August to 16 years, near the top of ransomware sentences, and South Korean agencies warned that North Korea's Lazarus Group is sharing tools with ransomware hackers.

wiki-artificial-intelligence.standing: A count of how many people open the English Wikipedia article on artificial intelligence each day. It is a rough gauge of public curiosity about the field rather than of the technology itself, rising when AI reaches audiences outside the industry.
wiki-artificial-intelligence.recent: The series peaked on Jul 17 and bottomed at 16,060 on Jul 25 without a clear cause in the record. The strongest recent story is the design of 16 working virus genomes by a Stanford model, reported on 07 Aug — the first viruses created by AI that are not found in nature.

wiki-russia.standing: Wikipedia's country article for Russia, and one of the most-read pages on the site. Daily readership rises when the country is in the news, which makes the series a rough gauge of how much of the world's attention Moscow is holding.
wiki-russia.recent: The rise into the 6 August peak tracked Ukraine's strikes on two Russian refineries, including Yaroslavl — the second such strike since July — and the US Senate's bill authorising tariffs on buyers of Russian oil, which lands on India, China and Turkey rather than Moscow. Zelenskyy then flew to Belgrade.

wiki-pakistan.standing: Daily readership of the English Wikipedia article on Pakistan, a nuclear-armed state of some 250 million people. Traffic to a country page tends to track the moments that country becomes the story rather than the backdrop.
wiki-pakistan.recent: Readership climbed toward the 7 August signing in Mecca, where Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan agreed a joint defence pact — described in some quarters as a 'Sunni NATO' — with Shehbaz and Munir meeting MBS in the bilateral, and each state's commitments still undefined. The 29 July peak came with reports of Chinese missiles bound for Iran.

wiki-china.standing: The Wikipedia article on China, the world's most populous state after India, its largest manufacturer and second-largest economy. Its pageview count is a rough gauge of how much general attention the country is drawing on any given day.
wiki-china.recent: Beijing spent the window legislating and restricting: a climate-only five-year plan, a national ethnic unity law codifying Xinjiang's campaign-era controls, and tightened drone export rules alongside sanctions on six US entities. Washington answered with a polysilicon price floor.

wiki-strait-of-hormuz.standing: One of the world's busiest waterways for oil, a narrow channel at the mouth of the Gulf through which a large share of seaborne crude and LNG must pass. Traffic through it sets the risk premium on energy far beyond the region.
wiki-strait-of-hormuz.recent: Transits fell by a third this week after a tanker reported two explosions near Hormuz and Iran and the US described control of the channel in incompatible terms. Oman, not Washington, is brokering a reopening, while Iraqi crude now moves overland through Syria and Aramco's profit rose 44%.

wiki-bitcoin.standing: Wikipedia's article on Bitcoin, and how many people open it each day. Readership of a reference page tends to move when the subject is doing something a general audience does not already understand — a crash, a split, a theft — rather than when it is merely expensive.
wiki-bitcoin.recent: The month's spike came at the end of a run of thefts: the Coldcard hack drained $120 million, a firmware bug let thieves take $88 million from a hardware-wallet maker in Toronto, and a sweep took 4,585 offline wallets for $89 million without any of them going online. Bitcoin fell 4% and sits 49% below its record.

wiki-saudi-arabia.standing: Daily readership of the Wikipedia article on Saudi Arabia — the kingdom that holds the largest share of the world's spare oil capacity and the two holiest sites in Islam. Attention to it rises when the Gulf's security order is in question.
wiki-saudi-arabia.recent: The 23 July peak came as Saudi Arabia joined US strikes on Iraq, entering the US–Iran war outright. Readership climbed again in August around the Mecca pact — a joint defence agreement with Turkey and Pakistan signed in Jeddah on 7 August — and Houthi missile strikes on Marib and Hadramout and on Najran, where 11 civilians were wounded.

wiki-donald-trump.standing: The Wikipedia article on the sitting US president, and one of the most-read biographies on the site. Its daily readership rises and falls with whatever the presidency is doing, which makes it a rough gauge of how much of the world's attention Washington is holding.
wiki-donald-trump.recent: Readership has cooled through a month dominated by Iran: Trump made the cancellation of a strike conditional rather than final on 2 August, then claimed the US fully controls the Strait of Hormuz while Tehran described the same channel differently. Since then the fights have been domestic — 25 states suing over tariffs, a renewed bid to fire Cook, a court halting the ballroom build.

wiki-india.standing: The English Wikipedia article on India, and a daily count of how many people open it. Attention to a country's reference page rises when that country does something the rest of the world has to react to.
wiki-india.recent: Readership held steady through a month in which India kept colliding with outside pressure: a US Senate bill threatening 100% tariffs over Russian oil turned into a domestic argument over strategic autonomy, Modi inaugurated the Param Pragya AI supercomputer, and New Delhi geoblocked Bitchat's GitHub code during a shutdown.

wiki-israel.standing: The daily count of people reading the English Wikipedia article on Israel — a rough gauge of how many ordinary readers are seeking background on the country rather than following a specific story, and one that rises when events pull in an audience outside the usual one.
wiki-israel.recent: Readership through the window tracked a widening war rather than a single event: strikes resumed in south Lebanon as Beirut and Israel met in Rome for a seventh round of direct talks, a drone hit a cemetery prayer area, and troops raided Qalandiya camp. In Gaza, rescuers pulled 112 bodies from one flattened block while Netanyahu rejected a withdrawal order.

wiki-united-states.standing: Wikipedia's article on the United States, and how many people open it each day. It is a rough gauge of global curiosity about the country — a background hum that lifts when Washington does something the rest of the world has to react to.
wiki-united-states.recent: The window is dominated by Washington and Iran. Trump halted planned attacks on Iran's infrastructure on 2 August, then claimed on 3 August that the US fully controls the Strait of Hormuz, with Iran, Oman and the US reported close to a Hormuz deal by 5 August. Trump also admitted months of strikes on Iran had strained US munitions stockpiles.

wiki-ukraine.standing: The Wikipedia article on Ukraine, and how many people open it each day. Attention to a country's basic page tends to move with war news rather than with anything about the country itself, which makes it a rough gauge of how far a conflict has spread beyond its own region.
wiki-ukraine.recent: The war widened past Ukraine's borders in the window: a Russian missile detonated in a Polish field on 30 July, sending NATO jets up, and on 5 August German police found an explosives-carrying drone that shut Leipzig's DHL runway. The same week Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv, killing 17, and Ukraine struck two Russian refineries.

wiki-lebanon.standing: The Wikipedia article on Lebanon, and the number of people who open it each day. Attention to a country's basic entry rises when something happens there that sends readers looking for context they do not already have.
wiki-lebanon.recent: The July peak fell in the week Israel and Lebanon agreed to move direct talks to Rome, with three villages designated a "pilot zone" and 13 disputed points on the Blue Line left unsettled. Readership has drifted down since, even as a drone struck a cemetery prayer area and UN rights chief Türk described a Gaza-like pattern in the south.

wiki-nigeria.standing: Daily readership of a Wikipedia country article — a rough gauge of how much of the world is looking up a place at all. It rises when a country enters the news somewhere far from it, and settles back to a baseline set by its size and diaspora.
wiki-nigeria.recent: The late-July peak came around the Osun election dispute, where the state police chief was booed off stage at a stakeholders' forum and Tinubu later ordered the EFCC to vacate a freeze on Osun's account. Attention has since eased through a quieter stretch of trafficking arrests and a coup-funding trail in Abuja.

cp:hormuz.standing: One-fifth of global seaborne oil passes through this 21-mile strait between Iran and Oman.
cp:hormuz.recent: Transits are running about half their 90-day baseline after the closure, with a tanker reporting two explosions near Kumzar and inbound ships facing an Iranian-controlled lane. Oman is brokering a reopening, and traders are rerouting: Iraqi crude now moves overland through Syria, while Gulf crude arriving in Malaysia has dropped.

cp:bab-el-mandeb.standing: Between Yemen and Djibouti — the Red Sea’s southern gate. Houthi attacks since 2023 have pushed container shipping to reroute around Africa.
cp:bab-el-mandeb.recent: Traffic has fallen with the war spreading from the Red Sea onto land and across the Saudi border: at least 12 missiles hit Hadramout and Marib on Friday, Houthis struck Saudi military deployments, and a projectile sank the Indian-flagged MSV Faize Noore Oliya. Crossings dropped to 18 on Sunday from 28 Friday.

cp:suez.standing: Egypt’s 120-mile artery carries roughly 12% of global trade. The 2021 closure disrupted supply chains for weeks; Red Sea instability keeps it volatile.
cp:suez.recent: Traffic is running at about half its 90-day baseline as attacks spread through the Red Sea approaches. A projectile strike sank the Indian-flagged MSV Faize Noore Oliya on 4 August, and ship traffic at Bab el-Mandeb — the canal's southern gate — dropped to 18 crossings on Sunday from 28 on Friday.

cp:malacca.standing: Between Malaysia and Sumatra — the fastest route between the Indian and Pacific Oceans. Over 80,000 ships a year, including most of China’s oil imports.
cp:malacca.recent: Traffic sits near its 90-day baseline after a July dip, with the strait's role reinforced by events elsewhere: Hormuz closure cut Gulf crude arriving in Malaysia, and Thailand shelved its Kra Isthmus land bridge, the transhipment scheme meant to offer an alternative to Malacca.

cp:taiwan.standing: Between mainland China and Taiwan — roughly 40% of the world’s container traffic passes through, and the flashpoint of any US–China confrontation.
cp:taiwan.recent: Traffic is running roughly level with its 90-day baseline, and the fall across the window is small. The swing between 28 vessels on Jul 10 and 401 on Jul 12 tracks rough seas rather than any closure, with waves up to 2.6m in the latest reading. Chinese coast guard ships also drifted off Orchid Island, east of Taiwan, on Jul 31.

cp:panama.standing: 50-mile shortcut between the Atlantic and Pacific. Drought in 2023–24 cut daily transits by half — a live example of climate binding to trade.
cp:panama.recent: Traffic sits at 27 vessels a day, a quarter below where the series opened and 4.1% under its own 90-day baseline, having fallen from 83 on 13 July to a low of 22 on 22 July. Nothing in the record explains the drop.

cp:bosporus.standing: Istanbul’s 20-mile waterway links the Black Sea to the Mediterranean — the only route for Russian naval access and Ukrainian grain exports.
cp:bosporus.recent: Traffic has thinned as the war moved onto the water: drones sank a Rosatom freighter near Novorossiysk on 1 August and struck the Turkish-operated Nadezhda days later, and Turkey's coast guard has since turned some Novorossiysk-bound vessels back. The CPC shutdown at the same port has halved Kazakh oil output this month.

cp:gibraltar.standing: 8 miles between Morocco and Spain — the only Atlantic–Mediterranean link. A surveillance chokepoint for Russian submarines and sanctioned oil.
cp:gibraltar.recent: Traffic has held near its 90-day baseline through the Ceuta crossings and the Schengen row above it: Spain and Italy are now policing each other's borders after Italy suspended free movement on 31 July, but the measures fall on travellers and documents, not hulls. Vessel counts moved 4% across the window, with seas calm at 0.7m.

cp:dover.standing: The busiest shipping lane on Earth — 400+ ships a day squeeze through the English Channel’s 21-mile narrows.
cp:dover.recent: Traffic has run close to its own 90-day baseline, with no weather or closure to disturb it. What has drawn attention to the strait instead is the crossing itself: on 4 August a dinghy carrying about 160 people caught fire mid-Channel off Boulogne-sur-Mer, prompting a major rescue operation.

cp:cape-of-good-hope.standing: The 3,000-mile detour around southern Africa — the alternative when the Red Sea is closed. The new default for tankers since Houthi attacks began.
cp:cape-of-good-hope.recent: Traffic swung hard across the window — from 35 vessels on May 11 to 161 on May 15 — and now sits at 97, about 7% below its own 90-day baseline. Rough seas, with waves to 3.7m, are the current drag; the input does not otherwise explain the swing.

cp:kerch.standing: Between Crimea and Russia — the only access to the Sea of Azov. A flashpoint since 2014 and contested throughout the Russia–Ukraine war.
cp:kerch.recent: Traffic has gone to zero, roughly 90 percent below its own 90-day baseline, after running at 50 vessels a day in mid-May. Turkey's coast guard has begun turning back some commercial vessels bound for Novorossiysk following attacks on Turkish-linked ships, and Ukraine has struck Russian refineries, including at Yaroslavl.

mkt:tadawul.standing: The Arab world’s largest exchange by market value, dominated by Aramco. Trades Sunday to Thursday, so it opens the global week before Tokyo.
mkt:tadawul.recent: The index sits below where it started the window despite Aramco's quarterly profit jumping on war-driven oil prices, and OPEC+ raising output quotas by 188,000 barrels daily. The drag is proximity to the fighting: Saudi Arabia joined US strikes in Iraq, Houthi missiles hit Marib and Hadramout and wounded 11 in Najran, and Riyadh signed a defence pact with Turkey and Pakistan while bracing for attack.

mkt:bist.standing: Türkiye’s only exchange. Priced in lira, so its index level carries the country’s inflation as much as its earnings — read the direction, not the number.
mkt:bist.recent: Turkey's coast guard began refusing some vessels passage toward Novorossiysk after drones struck the Nadezhda, a Turkish-operated cargo ship, putting a NATO member's own shipping and the Black Sea grain and crude trade at the centre of the war. Ankara also signed a collective-defence pact in Mecca with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.

mkt:dfm.standing: The Gulf’s main listing venue for property and banking. Moved from a Sunday–Thursday week to Monday–Friday in 2022, unlike Riyadh.
mkt:dfm.recent: Seven blasts in twenty minutes hit Jebel Ali port on 5 August, the transshipment hub the listed logistics and trade names depend on, and the same week brought reports of a Hormuz lane split that would route inbound ships through an Iranian-controlled lane. The index sits below its Jun 18 high of 6270.

mkt:bursa-malaysia.standing: The world’s largest market for Islamic finance instruments, and the centre of the global sukuk trade.
mkt:bursa-malaysia.recent: The index has drifted about 1.3% lower over the window, and the political ground has moved under it: a Malay-nationalist wave took Negeri Sembilan from Pakatan Harapan on 3 August, and the DAP is holding a vote on whether to stay in Anwar's unity government. Gulf crude arriving in Malaysia has dropped on the Hormuz closure.

mkt:idx.standing: The exchange of the world’s largest Muslim-majority country, heavily weighted to commodities and banking.
mkt:idx.recent: The index sits well below its May 7 high of 7,174, having bottomed at 5,342 on June 8. The clearest domestic shock in the window was Bank Indonesia governor Perry Warjiyo's surprise mid-term resignation on July 27, given without a stated reason and leaving succession open.

mkt:tse.standing: Asia’s largest exchange, and the first major market to price each trading day.
mkt:tse.recent: The index has been trading off the yen. Tokyo sold dollars for yen hours before the Bank of Japan held rates at 1% on 31 July, and a joint US-Japan intervention on 3 August pushed the dollar to a one-month low — a headwind for exporters after Toyota's quarterly profit hit $9.4 billion on the cheap yen.

mkt:hkex.standing: Where mainland Chinese companies meet foreign capital — the clearest daily read on sentiment toward China.
mkt:hkex.recent: Beijing sanctioned six US entities Wednesday alongside tighter drone export controls, and factory growth slowed to a four-month low in July as export orders grew while domestic demand cooled. China's steel stock is now old enough to recycle, cutting into iron ore demand. The index sits below its May 7 high of 26,630.

mkt:sse.standing: Mainland China’s main board. Largely closed to foreign investors, so it tracks domestic policy more than global risk appetite.
mkt:sse.recent: The index sits well below its May peak, with the July trough coming as factory growth slowed to a four-month low and domestic demand cooled while export orders grew. Policy has since turned outward and defensive: Beijing tightened drone export controls and sanctioned six US entities, and Washington set a price floor on polysilicon.

mkt:krx.standing: Dominated by Samsung and SK Hynix — a proxy for the global semiconductor cycle.
mkt:krx.recent: The index has swung with the memory cycle. It fell to 5,594 on 30 July, then posted its largest single-day gain ever — a record 18% — the next day on a chip rally, after Samsung reported chip profit up 250-fold and warned shortages would worsen. It slipped again on 7 August as SK Hynix dropped 5% on a $38B fab commitment.

mkt:bse.standing: Asia’s oldest exchange, founded 1875, and the benchmark for Indian equities.
mkt:bse.recent: The index sits near its Aug 6 high after climbing from the Jun 8 low, with policy news dominating the domestic tape: Parliament enabled merchant fees on the Unified Payments Interface, ending free public payments rails, and Modi inaugurated the Param Pragya AI supercomputer. The overhang is a US Senate bill threatening 100% tariffs on India.

mkt:sgx.standing: Southeast Asia’s financial hub, weighted to banks and regional property.
mkt:sgx.recent: The index climbed to a 5,713 high on Jul 29, days after Singapore's central bank tightened its currency band again — back-to-back tightening aimed at price risks in an economy exposed to an oil shock. Shipping through Bab el-Mandeb has stayed steady, with twenty ships crossing on Monday, unchanged.

mkt:twse.standing: TSMC alone is roughly a third of the index, which makes this the most concentrated major market on the map.
mkt:twse.recent: The index has recovered from a low on Jul 30 to 44,230, still well below its Jun 22 high of 47,740. The trade around it is narrow: chipmaking employs few of Taiwan's workers, a two-speed AI economy in which the fabs boom and the rest does not. Chinese coast guard ships patrolled east of Taiwan on Jul 31, off Orchid Island.

mkt:set.standing: Thailand’s benchmark, sensitive to tourism flows and regional energy prices.
mkt:set.recent: The index sits at its 50-day high of 1,639, reached on Jul 17, after climbing roughly 9% from a low of 1,484 on May 12. The Bangkok news of the period was political and social rather than corporate: Thailand shelved its Kra Isthmus land bridge on Jul 26, and welcomed Myanmar's Min Aung Hlaing on Aug 6.

mkt:pse.standing: A small, domestically-driven market where remittance flows move the index.
mkt:pse.recent: The index has climbed to a series high despite a run of South China Sea friction: joint Philippine-US-Japan drills followed water-cannon clashes at two shoals, and a venture-funded startup has been provoking Chinese warships. A magnitude 6.3 earthquake in the southern Philippines on 5 August did not interrupt the advance.

mkt:asx.standing: Mining and banking. Often the first major market to react to Chinese demand data.
mkt:asx.recent: The index sits near its high after a run of resource-sector news: China's steel stock is now old enough to recycle, shifting demand away from Australian iron ore, and a UN human rights complaint targets Australia's exported coal emissions rather than domestic ones. Separately, EVs reached 23.4% of June car sales.

mkt:jse.standing: Africa’s largest exchange by far, and the continent’s only one with a usable public daily series.
mkt:jse.recent: The index sits below where it started the window, having bottomed at 108,300 on Jul 23 before recovering. The domestic backdrop is one of rising costs rather than growth: electricity bills rose up to 14% this month after municipal surcharges, squeezing household budgets in Johannesburg.

mkt:b3.standing: Latin America’s largest exchange, driven by iron ore, oil and Brazilian rates.
mkt:b3.recent: The index has drifted down through a widening rupture between Brasília and Washington. Brazil denied visas to two senior US diplomats on 25 July, requested WTO consultations over US tariffs on 28 July, and Washington revoked the Brazilian ambassador's visa on 4 August, offering to restore it if Brasília accepts its envoy pick. Lula's nomination for a fourth term on 2 August added an election to the calendar.

mkt:bmv.standing: Mexico’s benchmark, tightly coupled to US demand and the peso.
mkt:bmv.recent: The index sits below where it started the window despite the day's rise, and the input does not identify what drove the move.

mkt:byma.standing: Priced in a currency that has lost most of its value repeatedly, so the index rises even in bad years. Direction over a day means something; the level does not.

mkt:tsx.standing: Energy, mining and banks — a commodity index wearing an equity index’s clothes.
mkt:tsx.recent: The index has climbed 7.5 percent over the past 64 days to close at a high on Aug 7. Nothing in the available material explains the move.

mkt:nyse.standing: The largest equity market on earth. Its close sets the tone every other market opens against.
mkt:nyse.recent: The index closed at a 63-day high on Aug 7, up 4.8% over the window, on a week dominated by Washington policy rather than earnings: the Senate advanced secondary tariffs on buyers of Russian oil, Treasury sanctioned Iranian dollar-token exchanges, and Trump renewed his bid to remove Fed governor Cook.

mkt:lse.standing: Most FTSE 100 revenue is earned abroad, so a falling pound tends to push the index up.

mkt:xetra.standing: Germany’s industrial and chemical base — Europe’s clearest export barometer.
mkt:xetra.recent: The index reached 26320 on Aug 7, a 6.7% climb over the window, despite deep cuts at its industrial names: BMW is cutting 8,000 jobs worldwide, Porsche another 5,000, and Mercedes cut its sales outlook on weak China. Banking consolidation is back in view as Commerzbank warms to UniCredit, and Adidas reported strong growth on the World Cup.

mkt:euronext-paris.standing: Luxury goods and energy dominate — unusually exposed to Chinese consumer demand.
mkt:euronext-paris.recent: The index reached 8715 on Aug 7, the high of the period, up 6.3% since the May 15 low. TotalEnergies agreed to buy Shell's entire European onshore renewables arm, and Air France-KLM filed a binding bid for TAP against Lufthansa. Wildfires and a heatwave that shut three of France's 57 reactors did not interrupt the climb.

mkt:euronext-amsterdam.standing: The world’s oldest exchange, now carried largely by ASML.
mkt:euronext-amsterdam.recent: The index sits near the top of its 67-day range, reaching 1112 on Aug 4 after climbing about 9% from a low of 999.4 on May 12. Little in the window explains the move directly; the one heavily reported corporate item was Shell's agreement to sell its European onshore renewables business on Aug 3.

mkt:bme.standing: Spanish banks with heavy Latin American exposure make this a proxy for both regions.
mkt:bme.recent: The index closed at a series high on Aug 6, having risen steadily through the summer, and slipped fractionally the next day. Nothing in the record ties the run to a single Spanish event: the news out of Madrid in the same window was Spain's imposition of reciprocal border checks on Italy after Italy suspended Schengen over the Ceuta arrivals.

mkt:borsa-italiana.standing: Banks and utilities, and the market most sensitive to Italian sovereign debt spreads.

mkt:six.standing: Nestlé, Roche and Novartis carry the index, which makes it defensive when the world turns risk-off.

mkt:nasdaq-stockholm.standing: Nordic industrials and telecoms, and a useful early read on European capital spending.
mkt:nasdaq-stockholm.recent: The index sits near the top of its 65-day range after climbing from a 15 May low of 3036 to a 5 August high of 3327, easing 0.3% on the day. The coverage in this window points at Volkswagen, where the controlling families broke board silence to press management over excess capacity — a signal to the European industrial complex Stockholm's exporters sit inside.

mkt:tase.standing: Trades Sunday to Thursday. Heavily weighted to banks, defence and technology.
mkt:tase.recent: The index sits at 4,066, roughly 8.5% below where it stood two months ago, after falling from a 4,477 high on May 8 to a 3,966 low on June 29 and recovering only partly since. Nothing in the available reporting accounts for the decline.
